utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Vujic. Yes, Mr. Tieger, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, in response to your question on the 2nd of October at transcript 48033, seeking clarity over the final brief's reference to Count 7 in relation to Srebrenica, Your Honours are correct. We have previously stated that Count 7 is not charged in relation to Srebrenica, and of course we maintain that position. We are grateful to Your Honours for the opportunity, therefore, to correct the record. We do not seek a finding that Karadzic is responsible for the crime of deportation, Count 7, in relation to Srebrenica. Additionally, after the Defence closing argument, the Trial Chamber inquired why the Prosecution could not make its declaration with respect to incidents and charges on which no evidence was presented after the closing argument, that is, in relation to 73 bis. So let me do so now accordingly. The Prosecution does not intend to proceed further with the incidents and charges against the accused which have been excluded pursuant to Rule 73 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Once we dealt with deportation, having heard all the evidence and also heard the closing arguments, what specific incidents are charged as deportation in municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it would be difficult to recite the totality. I mean, those would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could come back after the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. I mean, they would encompass basically the entirety of the overarching JCE. So I'll see if there's some compact way to define that for the Court's benefit, rather than by reference to the overall charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And when you come back, could you also address the Chamber as to the elements that distinguish deportation from forcible transfer, in particular in terms of the accused's mens rea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let me proceed, then, to address some of the positions taken by the accused during his closing submissions. At transcript 47885, Dr. Karadzic stated that he "did not introduce a state of war in Republika Srpska so that the life of ordinary citizens would not become militarised." That is false. Apart from the fact that it would have changed little for ordinary citizens - see, for example, P970, pages 104 and 334 - the real reason that Karadzic did not introduce a state of war was to make it easier to ensure that expelled non-Serbs would not return. And he explained this contemporaneously. In the context of an Assembly discussion in September 1992, that's at D456, a discussion about the borders of Republika Srpska and about ensuring separation from the Muslims and Croats. At that time, Karadzic distinguished between "external" borders, that is, those that separated Bosnia and Herzegovina from Serbia or the Serbian Krajina in Croatia, and "internal" borders, that is, those that would separate the Bosnian Serbs from Muslims and Croats within Bosnia. And he said: "We'll accept the external borders on condition that we get the internal borders, but we will do everything we can to make the internal borders thicker than the external ones without publicly saying so. Our borders towards the Muslims and Croats are to be thicker than our borders towards Serbia and Montenegro and the Serbian Krajina." D456, page 55. In other words, "thicker borders" separating Serbs from Muslims and Croats would prevent the Muslims and Croats from crossing those borders and changing the newly formed demographics. Karadzic then explained why a state of war had not been imposed, and that's at page 57. "We have refrained from introducing a state of war because it is much more important, more founded and feasible, if something is done by the civilian authorities without a state of war, under regular circumstances, such as settlement and resettlement. When the civilian authorities do this, it is much better, it is not discarded after the war." So contrary to Karadzic's claim to you last week that he refrained from introducing a state of war in order to normalise conditions of life in Republika Srpska, he did so to ensure the permanence of the forcible transfers that had been and were being carried out, reasoning that if people are moved out and resettled under the apparent auspices of the regular civilian authorities, then this will not be reversed after the war. Now, that alone is sufficient to expose as false Karadzic's claim that all citizens who left the territory could return to their homes when they wished, claims that were recognised by internationals at the time as "completely nonsense" because they were made in the context of ongoing ethnic cleansing. And see the paragraph 80 of the confidential Prosecution brief. But even if and even though Dr. Karadzic couldn't sell this to the internationals at the time, he now tries to sell it to you, repeating the claim multiple times in the course of his submissions. For example, T47899 and T48029. He claimed at 47899 that he "rejected the speech of the member of parliament who was saying that the refugees would not be able to return or that mosques were destroyed." And that after this meeting he signed a declaration enabling the return of refugees. This reference to his reaction to the speech at the Assembly session is another blatant mis-characterisation; the precise opposite is true. That deputy, Vjestica, did not say that the refugees would not be able to return; he was expressing concern that the latest peace proposal would permit them to come back. And Karadzic assured him and the Assembly that it was not true and there was no need to worry. As he explained: "This is what was said about the control of the borders. We will have barbed wire for ten years." P1379, pages 25 through 26. As Karadzic stated at the 46th Assembly, P1403, page 157, his forces had created new demographic realities that he intended to maintain. "We have created new realities. If you want to give Zvornik to the Muslims, then you have to wage a new war in order to expel those Serbs back to Zenica." And Karadzic assured his followers that he would maintain that reality despite any purported commitment to return required by international agreements. So when the deputy -- the president of the Deputies' Club Vojo Maksimovic advocated that non-Serbs be openly banned from returning to areas under Serb control and expressed concern that aspects of the peace proposals would trigger the return of Muslims and Croats, stating: "Any thought about having 500 or more Muslims within our future country is out of the question." P1385, pages 126 through 127. When he expressed that concern, Karadzic explained the strategy that would provide lip service to the principle of return but frustrate it in practice. "As to the return of the refugees, I owe an answer to Vojo's question. According to international law, we have no right to ban the return of the refugees. In principle, all refugees can return, but I would just add one sentence. This also has to be a two-way process." Karadzic recalled that a puzzled Owen had asked: "Why do you insist on a two-way process?" And then Karadzic explained it to the Assembly: "When the Serbs from Zvornik return to Zenica, then the Muslims from Prijedor will return to Prijedor. Therefore, it must be a two-way process." That's at page 132 of that session. And just in case that wasn't clear enough, he explained it again at a subsequent Assembly session, the 53rd Assembly in 1995, when the same issue was presented by the latest peace plan's inclusion of language regarding "the right of refugees and displaced persons to be able to return to their homes." Karadzic again emphasised that the RS would insist on "an overall process." And he explained how this overall process would effectively prevent non-Serbs from returning. "That means that the Muslims from Kozluk can return to Kozluk, if the Serbs from Kozluk return to Zenica. If they don't want to return, then we need -- and if they cannot return, then we need a new war to exchange that, and that's why I think we should always insist on this. So an overall process, either overall or none at all." Karadzic then pointed out the cleverness of his ploy. "We can act the Serbian Cyrillic way and tell it to their face or we can be a bit cunning. We do have to be a bit cunning." Karadzic's cunning approach fooled no one then and should not fool you now. At transcript 47861 Karadzic challenged the Prosecution's position about the Cutileiro Plan, stating: "We accepted the maps and I had to tell the MPs that we were not accepting the maps because otherwise we would have had a very difficult situation in parliament." Cutileiro, Karadzic's witness, made clear that Karadzic's claim that he "accepted the maps" is false. Cutileiro explained that the map that was attached to the Statement of Principles was "a preliminary map" which merely reflected the existing, absolute, and relative majorities in the municipalities across Bosnia. That's T33962 and 33965. There was nothing to accept or not accept; it was the existing situation and therefore the starting point for any further discussions. It was obvious, as Cutileiro testified, that any discussion of what territory would be encompassed by what entity would be a source of major upcoming dispute. And therefore, Cutileiro explained, it was going to be the object of a Working Group to define borders precisely "but that work was never done." That's at T33961. And although Karadzic insists on the contrary to you now, he never put that to his own witness, Cutileiro, and never attempted to suggest that Cutileiro was wrong when he said nothing moved beyond the meaningless map that was attached to the Statement of Principles. Cutileiro also made clear that the -- that those negotiations never reached the agreement stage. The agreement in principles was merely a preliminary step toward further negotiations. That's at T33955. Karadzic himself emphasised at the time that the agreement was not final, that is, the Statement of Principles was not a final agreement, and made clear that he never intended to honour even those preliminary principles. He reassured the Assembly first that the document "is not final" and it "has not been signed." That's at D90, page 6. He emphasised that he would "never have signed this paper as a document, never, never, never." That's at D90, page 43. One of the reasons the agreement in principles was unacceptable to Karadzic was that, as Cutileiro confirmed at T33958, it contemplated that Bosnia would be a single state. In February 1995, after Karadzic had succeeded in forcibly creating a largely mono-ethnic Serb state, he recalled: "The first principle or the first position in all Cutileiro principles, if you remember, was that Bosnia was a state consisting of this and that, but it always said that Bosnia was a state and we never accepted that." That's at P1407, page 116. Karadzic's repeated invocation of the Cutileiro Agreement to justify the implementation of the common criminal purpose is not only conceptionally flawed but grounded on falsehoods. And speaking of falsehoods, at T47867, Karadzic said: "And the table made by Ewa Tabeau shows that more Muslims left municipalities after the Dayton Accords than before. When the war was over, when the borders were clear, people started moving. Until then, they stayed, although they had the option to sign up for convoys and didn't use that option." This astonishing claim is based on a manipulation of one of Dr. Tabeau's tables during cross-examination at T28349 through 71, when Karadzic asked about the percentage of people who left after the war in comparison to the percentage who left between 1991 and 1995. Perhaps we can use Prijedor and Sanski Most, two municipalities I discussed last week, as examples of this manipulation. So as you can see, according to P5010, page 4, table 2, as well as Tabeau's testimony at T28169 through 70, there were 49.351 Muslims in Prijedor in 1991. 42.000 had moved out by 1993 and 3.600 remained in 1995. Equally, according to the table, 28.136 Muslims were in Sanski Most in 1991; 24.000 had moved out by 1993; and approximately 3350 were left in 1995. Now, although the RS sources for the mid-conflict figures are different sources than Tabeau's statistical sources, these figures unmistakably reveal that the vast majority of Muslims were gone by 1995. But not to Dr. Karadzic, who insisted on pointing out in cross-examination the percentage of decline between 1995 and 1997, a highly misleading and meaningless figure because by far the biggest part of the population change took place before. And indeed, if you check the Prijedor statistics, even that claim is factually in error, even that meaningless claim, because in fact in Prijedor, the percentage between 1995 and 1997 is slightly higher than the percentage before. In any event, Dr. Karadzic now trots out this irrelevant argument again, this time dressing it up as if it was about raw numbers instead of percentages, and hoping no one will notice. This is as disingenuous as saying that you're happy for everyone to return even as you're kicking them out, and hoping no one will notice. And we'll see more of this approach when we discuss his Sarajevo arguments. Your Honours, some points were raised regarding Count 1 of the indictment. Now, first, contrary to the Defence suggestion, this count does not turn on any specific pieces of evidence that the Appeals Chamber cited as examples, examples that alone were sufficient to support a 98 bis finding. Those were merely exemplars for the totality of the evidence supporting the finding. In any event, the thrust of the Defence submission is that the Chamber should essentially defer to or is constrained by the findings in other cases, including Brdjanin, Stakic, and even the Eichmann case. As you have noted previously and as the Appeals Chamber itself noted in response to essentially the same argument, that's found at para 94 of their decision, this Chamber must adjudicate Count 1 based on the totality of the evidence on the record in this case. In assessing the intent of the accused, it is necessary to consider, amongst the totality of that evidence, the inference that arises from acts attributable to him. Many of the destructive acts against the Muslim and Croat communities were committed by his army and his police. By contrast, none of the accused in previous cases were the president of the RS and supreme commander. Indeed, Karadzic himself elicited evidence from both Stakic and Brdjanin that underscores their more limited authority over those organs. He led evidence, for instance, that Stakic could not issue orders to the army or the police, that's D4195 at paras 20 through 21, organs that Stakic acknowledged were responsible for widespread destructive acts, that's T45220 through 22. And he led evidence that Brdjanin did not have command authority over the army, that's D4034 at paragraph 38. Karadzic is now attempting to draw analogies to their cases, analogies that are rendered inapt by virtue of the very evidence that he led. Additionally, the Defence ignores that the Stakic case did not involve a vertical JCE going up to Karadzic, although the Trial Chamber in that case went out of its way to note the indications that there was one. That's trial judgement at para 551. Yet, while Stakic did not command the army and police that participated so significantly in destructive acts in Prijedor, the Stakic Appeals Chamber found, based on the evidence in that case, that a reasonable Trial Chamber could have found Stakic responsible for genocide, although it was not prepared to overturn the Trial Chamber's determination. The Defence also cited the Eichmann case, asserting that the failure to convict Eichmann of genocide for the two-year period when Jews were deported rather than exterminated supports the Defence position. It does not. The Eichmann case, which distinguished between the period of deportations and the commencement of exterminations, merely confirms the obvious, that forcible transfer alone does not constitute genocide, as I observed in our closing submissions. And one or two genocidal acts appended to forcible transfer would not ipso facto transform it into genocide. But that is very far from the case here, with thousands and thousands of genocidal acts. In citing the Eichmann case, the Defence attempts to suggest that this is a deportation rather than a genocidal case, as if they are somehow mutually exclusive. Genocidal intent often embraces the forcible displacement of a significant segment of the population. You need look no further than the Srebrenica precedents from this Tribunal to clearly see that destructive acts and forcible transfer can combine very effectively to reflect genocidal intent. As Judge Shahabuddeen stated: "... standing alone, forcible transfer did not constitute genocide, but in this case the transfer did not stand alone ... it was part - an integral part - of one single scheme to commit genocide involving killings, forcible transfer, and destruction of homes." That's the Krstic appeal judgement, separate opinion of Judge Shahabuddeen at paragraph 35. The determination of genocidal intent arises from, in addition to direct evidence from the mouth of the accused, the combined effect of the acts that the accused intentionally inflicted on the community and its foundations of life. An assessment of that combined intent on the community necessarily embraces forcible displacement, in addition to killings and other genocidal acts. Similarly, Your Honours, it does not matter if the motive for destruction, for example, to create a "secure" ethnically separate territory, is one that might have been achieved through means other than the destruction of the community. The issue is the intent that accompanies the genocidal and other destructive acts. And when one kills thousands, traumatises, imprisoned, debilitates thousands more, destroys most homes and sacral objects, and scatters group members to the winds, the intent to destroy that community inescapably follows. Finally, the Defence does something here that they did throughout the course of their submissions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before going further, Mr. Tieger. You distinguished the accused's case from the cases of Stakic and Brdjanin. How would you distinguish his case from the case of Krajisnik then?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, with -- first of all, you'd have to look at the precise evidence in the case, but as you are well aware from Mr. Krajisnik's testimony here, he -- he was not the supreme commander of the military and he purported not to be, that I don't -- the evidence in that case reflected in the judgement did not turn on that sort of finding. Further, the expressions of intent came directly out of this accused's mouth, not his. There are a battery of distinctions in that -- in that particular case, aside from the nuances of the particular evidence and the totality of the evidence which the Court in that case had to assess. Further, this Court would have to -- if making such a distinction indeed had relevance - and I would suggest it does not - then this Court would have to determine the extent to which that -- any previous Trial Chamber may have become caught up in the supposed dichotomy between forcible transfer and genocide, without appreciating the contribution that forcible transfer may make to establishing genocidal intent. So there are many ways of distinguishing the Krajisnik case, but as I mentioned before, it is for this Chamber based on the totality of the evidence which is unprecedented, I would suggest, whether or not the genocidal acts attributable to Dr. Karadzic were accompanied by the requisite intent. Mr. President, I was indicating -- I'm sorry. I don't know if the Court wanted to continue with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was waiting for the translation. Please continue. Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I had mentioned motive and then the focus -- and then the fact that the focus needs to be on the intent, not the motive. Then I went on to say that there was an effort by the Defence to do something we see permeating their submissions, and that was the attempt to suggest an innocuous interpretation for Dr. Karadzic's repeated statements about the extinction, annihilation, and bloodshed that awaited Bosnian Muslims and Croats. And in doing so, he asked Your Honours to look at the evidence piecemeal, divorced from the overall pattern of crimes that took place. Now, taken in isolation, both from other statements and also, more importantly, from the overall context, the significance and meaning of those statements might theoretically be susceptible of various interpretations. But those statements did not occur in isolation. They were made by the most powerful leader of the Bosnian Serbs, a man at the helm of the forces that would implement his policies through countless destructive acts against the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat communities. Those acts, which reveal an unmistakable intent to destroy the foundations of life of those communities, blow away any fanciful interpretations of Dr. Karadzic's statements and confirm them as direct expressions of his intent. Mr. President, Your Honours, let me turn to some of the Defence submissions on Sarajevo, and on the heels of the discussion about the attempted manipulation of Tabeau's statistics, let me first turn to another effort at statistical charlatanism. The accused claimed, with respect to Markale I, that Dr. Zecevic asserted that the projectile entered at a 60-degree angle and claimed a margin of error of 33 per cent. That's his claim. That means, according to Dr. Karadzic, that it could have been between 40 degrees and 79.8 degrees, a "huge range," and therefore it "could have been fired by anyone but the Chinese." That's at T48005. These statistics have nothing to do with Zecevic's analysis and everything to do with Karadzic's special statistical manipulations. Follow how he gets there. One, based on the configuration of the surrounding buildings, all agree that the minimum and maximum at which the projectile might have descended was between 50 degrees and the very steep 85 degrees, that is, somewhere within this 35-degree range. Two, Zecevic actually calculated that the projectile descended at a 60-degree angle, plus or minus 5 degrees. Three, Dr. Zecevic's 10-degree margin of error reflected approximately 33 per cent of the total 35-degree range, a margin of error that Karadzic's expert Allsop agreed was "generous." Four, with no mathematical or evidentiary basis whatsoever, Karadzic then reapplies that 33 per cent to Zecevic's 60-degree finding, angle of descent finding, coming up with a new range of error of nearly plus or minus 20 degrees and attributing it to Zecevic, when in fact Zecevic actually said it was plus or minus 5. And all of that tortured logic is an effort to obscure the important fact which is that when Dr. Karadzic's expert Dr. Allsop was asked whether Zecevic's generous margin of error of plus or minus 5 degrees addressed all of Allsop's concerns about possible variables and therefore allowed for a sufficiently accurate determination of the fire distance, when Dr. Allsop was asked that he answered that it did. That's at T29508 through 09. During his submissions regarding Sarajevo, Dr. Karadzic made generalised claims of alleged selectivity by the Prosecution, finally attempting to distill it with an alleged example at T48007. He claimed that the Prosecution failed "in full" a document in which the last omitted line reveals the opposite of what is claimed. But the reality is that it is Karadzic, once again, who omits the critical portion of the document. Now, he was referring to an excerpt from Banbury's diary quoting him as saying, that is quoting Karadzic as saying: "Retaliation is productive. When they shell Doboj and we retaliate, it's effective." You see that on the screen in front of you. And he showed the Court that slide, the slide which shows General Janvier confronting Karadzic with the fact that this retaliation targeted civilians and Karadzic ostensibly denying it, claiming: "No, military targets." And this supposedly reflected a classic form of cheating, according to Karadzic, by the Prosecution. But what he didn't show you are the very next lines of this very page, lines which show that this denial was completely superficial and disingenuous, and those lines are shown here. As Banbury explained, when Janvier disagreed with Karadzic, based on what was by that point, that is, in late April 1995, the very obvious fact that shelling in Sarajevo targeted civilians, Karadzic simply switched tacks, moving from a false denial to brushing off the shelling of civilians by his forces with a joke and a big laugh. "Maybe some of our gunners have bad eyes, (laughs big)." In short, in order to falsely create the impression that the Prosecution misleadingly cited a document which was actually favourable to him, Karadzic employed the very tactic that he falsely accused the Prosecution of using. Not content with this brazen falsehood he goes on to argue that only the Muslim side "could benefit from the suffering of Sarajevo." And therefore, there would be no reason for him to engage in terror. That's T48007. Of course, this is directly refuted by the very exchange we just discussed with Janvier, during which Karadzic noted that the shelling of Sarajevo to retaliate against the other side for events elsewhere was "an effective" strategy. Similarly, in March 1995, Mladic told General Smith that the intensified sniping of civilians in Sarajevo was in retaliation for Serb military casualties. That's at P2451, paras 94 through 95, and T13330. And Galic threatened Richard Mole several times that if events elsewhere did not go in the Serbs' favour, the city would be shelled. For example, telling Mole on one occasion that if the shelling from Igman on to Lukavica did not halt, he would "fire his weapons on to the city of Sarajevo." P1426, paras 92 through 94. As Mole described the situation more generally: "There was an accepted norm that if the Serb side failed to achieve their objectives - and I use that in the widest sense, in BH, so that anything from a local complaint to something else that happened within Bosnia - the general perception, which I shared, was that Sarajevo would suffer as a result." And Mole explained that this was understood to mean that artillery fire would be brought to bear on the city in response. P1426, para 91. Mole's observation was echoed by witness after witness. I refer to the evidence cited in our brief at para 609 and the concrete examples of Serb forces retaliating by shelling civilian areas of Sarajevo, as described in paragraph 736. Karadzic's claim that the Serb side did not benefit from the terror campaign is false. He himself confirmed the opposite, as did his subordinates, and international military officials watched it happen. At transcript page 8170, Karadzic invoked Bosnian army General Karavelic in support of his assertion that the SRK used shelling appropriately to neutralise enemy firing positions, a wildly misleading claim that was exposed during trial when it was revealed that Karavelic said in full: "Throughout the war, the Serb forces made no distinction between military and civilian targets. Anything that moved, including civilian pedestrians, came under fire. Hospitals, schools, and historical buildings received direct artillery, tank and mortar fire on a regular basis, while houses, apartments and gathering places, such as markets and waterlines, would be shelled without seeming pattern. Nobody knew when and where a shell would hit, so every place was dangerous." Fraser explained that this description by Karavelic "distinctly resembles the pattern that we saw" during his tour of duty. That's at T8170. Dr. Karadzic also spoke about what a "terrible" and "catastrophic" weapon multiple-barrel rocket-launchers were, insisting that the SRK never used these rockets. That's at T48015. And while they were not typically used, he should nevertheless make that claim to the parents of the 4-year-old girl killed in a rocket attack on the city centre in late August 1995. And for that see P1953, paras 98 through 100. In any event, Karadzic's acknowledgement that rockets should never be used in a place like Sarajevo confirms the inherently inappropriate and inaccurate weapons system upon which modified air bombs were based, and of course it cannot be reconciled with Karadzic's case that they somehow became less "terrible" and "catastrophic" when affixed to a 100- or 250-kilo air bomb. Your Honours, I now need to move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Karadzic also attacked the professionalism and objectivity of local Sarajevo police investigators, relying on sweeping generalisations to do so. His specific attack is reserved for an unscheduled sniping incident at Nehru Street. That's at T47958 through 59. Karadzic complains that the bullet's vertical trajectory was upward by 70 centimetres across a 2.5 metre room, presumably suggesting an angle that meant the fire was too close to be a Serb position, and that the horizontal trajectory was not calculated but would have revealed that fire had not come from a Serb position if it had been calculated. Again, both claims are wildly false. As reflected in P1911, Karadzic has not just doubled or tripled the actual upward trajectory but exaggerated by a factor of nine, by nine times, claiming that the bullet went up 70 centimetres when it went up only 8, producing an angle of fire actually of 1.4 degrees. Further, contrary to Karadzic's claim, the investigators in fact calculated the horizontal trajectory using a tried and true method. As KDZ477 testified, they used a piece of string to connect the entry and lodging points, thus identifying the trajectory, which pointed to where the bullet came from: SRK territory in Dobrinja 1. That's T10977. Karadzic's remaining arguments about local investigators, T47989 through 91, are actually groundless, amounting to a very general statement such as "the witness made mistakes" and then offering, through naked citations, what is essentially a cut-and-paste of large portions of examination, which he then dumps in the lap of the Trial Chamber to guess what it means and what significance should be attached to it. These broad allegations are replete with mis-characterisations. Many of the occasions where he claims a witness made a mistake are actually responses where the witness undermined the premise of Karadzic's question itself. Rather than revealing "mistakes" by the witness, they reveal failures of cross-examination by Karadzic. For instance, Karadzic alleges that one of Nedzib Djozo's many so-called "mistakes" included his evidence at T9607 through 09 that there were more than a hundred sniping victims attacked from the SRK's position in Spicasta Stijena. Karadzic then said: "I will put it to you that there weren't even ten in total." To which the witness responded: "That is a ridiculous statement. We know exactly how many people were killed. We kept a record." There was no impeachment and Karadzic moved on. Later on redirect examination at T9644 through 46, the Prosecution tendered P1991, the Stari Grad log-book showing dozens of killed sniping victims in Sedrenik, including children and the elderly. This shows that what Karadzic considers to be a mistake is instead examples where a witness disagreed with him, and where the witness was clearly right. But this was just one of many such examples of citations he gave for alleged mistakes of local investigators in Sarajevo. He claimed, as another example, that Sead Besic committed "cardinal errors" and then relies on examples such as T9439 through 40, where Karadzic simply disagrees with the witness about whether it was appropriate to move bodies after Markale I. Likewise at 9458 through 64, Karadzic's cross-examination fell apart as he attempted to show that a photograph depicted a different stabiliser based on its length. The witness demonstrated that when the stabiliser was laid flat on a table next to a ruler from above, as in the photo, it looked shorter than in reality due to the tail fins which raised the back of the stabiliser. And the witness then identified distinctive markings that matched the stabiliser in the photo with the stabiliser in court. This was clearly not a "mistake" by the witness, but a mistake in perception by Dr. Karadzic. He lists transcript pages, as another example, from KDZ166's testimony to show alleged "mistakes." Such as T8295, again, there's no mistake. The witness simply stated that his personal task was not to establish the direction of fire, but that this was for the ballistics team on -- the ballistics experts on the investigation teams. Or T8316 through 17, Karadzic asked the witness whether he was aware that ABiH launched a military offensive the day before the SRK's modified air bomb attack in scheduled incident G15, and the witness said: "No, I was a police officer. I was not an army member." Again, not a "mistake." Or T8321, no mistakes here either. Karadzic tried to get the witness to agree that a wire factory was actually making shells and the witness said he didn't know. The same is true of Karadzic's claim that KDZ477's findings were "unusable." At T9 -- 10944 through 47, cited by Dr. Karadzic, the witness simply explained that he personally was not a ballistics expert. Again, no mistake. At T980 the witness said: "In such a situation you always use a string to carry out that measurement. However, I didn't have to write that in my diary, that a string was used for it. It simply had to be done in order to establish where the bullet came from." Mr. President, are we proceeding for an hour at a time or an hour and a half?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In relation to attacks on the investigators, just two more examples of what Dr. Karadzic considers a mistake. He said that Dragan Miokovic committed "mistakes which disqualify everything that he provided to this case." But it is not even clear from the citations he offers what part of the testimony he could conceivably consider a mistake, such as at T8591 through 92 or 8631 through 633, with the latter passage concluding with the Presiding Judge admonishing Dr. Karadzic that his line of questioning involving "asking the witness to draw meaningless lines is unhelpful." Similarly, he claims that Emir Turkusic made mistakes, for example at 9066 through 69. And that passage concludes with a comment from the Presiding Judge that it was unclear what point Karadzic was even trying to mistake. The quote was from the Presiding Judge: "What I wanted you to do was repeat your question instead of wrapping up on your part. What was your question? It's not clear to us what the question was and what the answer was." And he made similar unfounded attacks on the credibility of international witnesses. For instance, at T47980, he falsely accused Jeremy Bowen of lying about the position of Serb gunners. In fact, Bowen frankly acknowledged at the outset of his testimony that he had made a mistake as to the location of the shooter of a busload of children in one of his stories, a mistake caused by the fact that he had been in the city a short time. And Bowen emphasised that the mistake had "no bearing" on the overall truth of the report. That's found at T10079 and 10081. In another example, at T47974, Karadzic falsely claimed that Banbury "admitted" that "the Muslim side had actually carried out tricks in order to deceive the international community." And he accused Banbury of failing to put that in his original statement. In fact, as can be shown at 13369 through 70, Banbury agreed only that the Bosnian Serb authorities made these kinds of allegations and that he took note of their "warnings." Similarly, Karadzic tried and failed to undermine Harland's evidence by asserting at T47976 that Harland "said in his own words he was there to defend the government and the measures and the agreements did not apply to the government forces." He cited to transcript page 2066 and paragraphs 31 to 33 of Harland's amalgamated statement, neither reference contains any evidence even remotely supporting this proposition. Mr. President, let me now turn to the accused's submissions related to Srebrenica. First, an isolated or a preliminary matter. At transcript pages 48024 to 48028, Karadzic argued that the Srebrenica-related graves included victims from prior to 1995. P4841 is a BiH Federal Commission for Missing Persons list of persons exhumed in Bosnia in various municipalities, including Zvornik, between 1996 and 2007. And I refer you also to P4837 at paragraphs 31, 64, and 72. Karadzic points to individuals whose disappearance predates 1995 and argues that they should be discounted from the total number of 1995 Srebrenica victims, but that reasoning is flawed. The individuals on P4841 whose disappearance predates 1995 were not counted by Janc and do not form part of the total figure of 5.977 victims in Srebrenica-related graves. And for that see the Srebrenica Narrative, paragraphs 170 through 171. Two individuals listed at P4841, at lines 2025 and 2128, have dates of disappearance listed as 12 July 1990 and 12 July 1905, respectively. It is clear that the year of disappearance listed there or recorded there for those two individuals is an obvious data entry error and, in fact, the ICMP records their date of disappearance as July 1995. And for that see P5913. I can also direct Your Honours' attention to P4771 at page 145, line 294, and P107 -- and page 107, rather, line 18. But let me move on to the bulk of the Srebrenica submissions by the accused. What is the Defence case? Mr. Robinson said in his submissions on Thursday that thousands of Bosnian Muslim prisoners were executed by the likes of Frank Kos and Drazen Erdemovic. That's T47952 through 53. He claims that a reasonable inference is that "Karadzic never planned or ordered those executions," that they were "concealed from him," and that he is therefore "not guilty of genocide." That's T47938 and see also 47947, lines 16 through 17. He went on to claim, referring to the 2 August intercept in which Beara and Stevo talk about getting back from the Republic of Serbia Muslim men who had fled across the River Drina, that Beara may have been saying that it would be no good if Karadzic agreed to exchanges and then the lack of prisoners from Srebrenica became known and that this shows that Karadzic had no knowledge that the prisoners would be executed or had been executed. And Mr. Robinson added: "And there were reasons for people in the VRS to have concealed executions from President Karadzic," T47947. It seems that Mr. Robinson is arguing that Beara and the VRS were concealing executions from Karadzic and this is also what is said or implied in the Defence brief, paragraphs 3039, 3110, 3114, 15, 53, 81 through 84, 3257, 3259 through 60, 80 through 81, 85, and 98. Who is Karadzic blaming? He said on Thursday: "Now what happened when they entered Srebrenica? I saw a few killings of some people who happened to be there by members of that well-known platoon and the members of this platoon took part in the killing of POWs." T48022. He was referring to the 10th Sabotage Detachment. Then he said: "None of my generals or ministers should even have been indicted, let alone convicted and sentenced to very long terms of imprisonment. It is justice that was condemned." T48025 through 26. So is Karadzic blaming Colonel Beara as Mr. Robinson does? Does the Defence blame Mladic and the VRS Main Staff or not? What is the Defence case? In any event, blaming Beara, who told KDZ320 that his orders to get rid of the Muslim prisoners in Zvornik came from "two presidents," that's found at our brief at 992 through 5, and who told Stevo in the 2 August intercept that they now had to tell our chief and the supreme chief, that is, Mladic and Karadzic, blaming Beara does not exculpate Karadzic. But both Mr. Robinson and Mr. Karadzic blame executioners like Frank Kos and Drazen Erdemovic, both of whom were members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, a unit that was directly subordinated to Mladic, see paragraph 823 of our brief, under the command and control therefore of General Mladic and Radovan Karadzic. And on the 16th of July, 1995, eight members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, including Kos and Erdemovic, travelled under orders from their base in Dragasevac to the Zvornik Brigade headquarters. From there, they were taken to Branjevo Farm, where they executed over 1.000 Muslim men. Beara told them in the immediate aftermath of the executions: "You have done a great job and the state will be grateful to you." See 1014 through 1020 of our brief. And the Republika Srpska state was grateful to them. In January 1996, the VRS and MUP leadership, including Dragan Kijac, then minister of the interior, collaborated to protect members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment from arrest and transfer to the ICTY, by issuing them fake IDs. That's at our brief paragraph 1070. On the 22nd of March, 1996, Karadzic had a meeting with Mladic, see 1058 through 59 and 1071 through 74 of our brief. US Secretary of State Albright had just visited the execution and burial site at Branjevo Farm, which is in the Pilica area. Karadzic talked about this in his closing and he said: "Nothing did happen in Srebrenica. My attention is being drawn to Srebrenica and to civilians, and whatever is happening happened 80 to 100 kilometres away from Srebrenica and it wasn't happening to civilians. And of course when we got the most convincing evidence, these mortal remains on the surface, when Madeleine Albright found this, then there were orders to investigate that and the military prosecutor said no one know anything about this and no one wants to know anything about this. There was an immediate response." That's at T48023. And Karadzic was not being honest. Remember the contemporaneous statement and record made by Mladic in his diary of what Karadzic said following Albright's visit: "A big show was put on for Albright. She expected they would find 1200 Muslim bodies at Pilica, but they found some five bodies." That's P1490, page 47. When Karadzic said that Albright expected to find 1200 bodies, he was referring to an account of the Branjevo Farm executions which had appeared in the Bosnian press that day, an interview with Drazen Erdemovic, one of the executioners whom he and Mr. Robinson blame. That's P6451. Karadzic's subordinates put on a "big show" for Albright. It is clear that he knew then that the bodies of the Muslim men and boys had been removed from the mass grave at Branjevo Farm and reburied months earlier. That's why they only found "some five bodies" as Karadzic said. On the following day, 23 March 1996, Karadzic ordered the VRS Main Staff and MUP to set up a "mixed expert commission" of three members each "to fully investigate and determine the facts regarding the alleged discovery of two decomposed bodies at the scene of earlier battles with the Muslim side in the Pilica area, Zvornik municipality." That's P3163, pages 6 and 8. This is the order to which Karadzic referred in his closing at T48023. But there were no battles in the Pilica area, see T23537. There were only mass executions of unarmed Muslim prisoners. Karadzic's order was a sham, part of the cover-up. The commission's membership, the MUP and VRS, assured that there would be no real investigation and there wasn't. This was confirmed by a meeting on 25 March chaired by Dragomir Vasic. A military prosecutor, Drinic, who attended the meeting "by accident," reported after: "None of the people present knew any details of the locality and of the actions that needed to be undertaken nor was anyone informed about what would be found on site, or else no one wanted to know." See our brief at 1074 and P3163. Karadzic alluded to this evidence in his closing at T48023. There was never an investigation or prosecution by either the VRS or MUP into the Srebrenica events, nor was there ever intended to be. See paragraph 1054 of our brief. I also refer you to paragraph 1075 and remind you of Karadzic's 1 April 1996 order for another investigation that was never intended to happen and the evidence related to that. In the Srebrenica component, as in the other aspects of the case, the Defence seeks to have you consider evidence in isolation, detached from the totality of the evidence. Let's just take one of the "facts" that Mr. Robinson drew to your attention last week. "Fact: Dr. Karadzic spoke with Miroslav Deronjic on 13 July at 2010. Deronjic informed him that they had 2.000 and there would be more during the night. Dr. Karadzic said that all goods must be placed in the warehouses by 12.00 tomorrow, not in warehouses there but somewhere else. Deronjic said he understood." Mr. Robinson went on to say that a reasonable inference is that Karadzic was referring to sending the prisoners to Batkovic, not Zvornik where they were delivered for death. Mr. Robinson asked rhetorically how Deronjic could possibly understand that the prisoners were to go to Zvornik and that Batkovic was the likely place in view of Milenko Todorovic's testimony that they received instructions at one point to prepare Batkovic prison to receive prisoners from Srebrenica. But let's tether to the totality of the evidence the extraordinary fact that Karadzic told Deronjic that all the goods, that is, 2.000 men and more to come, must be placed in the warehouses by 12.00 tomorrow, not there but somewhere else. Fact: By the time of this call, Mladic had given an order that the Bosnian Muslim men were to be moved to Zvornik to be killed. See paragraphs 955 and 966 of our brief. Fact: Deronjic told Beara that it was Karadzic's instructions that the Muslim men were to be moved to Zvornik. See paragraph 965 of our brief. Fact: At this meeting, the only issue was where - was where, not if - the prisoners were to be killed, that is, the meeting where Deronjic spoke to Beara. That's at our brief at footnote 3495. Fact: By 7.00 p.m. preparations were commencing for receipt of the thousands of prisoners that were being sent to Zvornik to be shot. See paragraphs 956 and 957 of the confidential brief. Fact: Todorovic's evidence is that he had instructions from Tolimir to prepare Batkovic camp and then was told by Tolimir to stop preparations. See our brief at footnote 3488. It is crystal clear that the supreme commander was instructing his subordinate what to do in that phone call. Clear he was telling him what to do and clear it was done. The "reasonable inference" posited by the Defence is that every single institution of state, the army, the police, the civilian authorities, ignored the supreme commander's instructions and then engaged in a lavish conspiracy of silence to ensure that no one told him, including his trusted commissioner. Mr. President, Your Honours, I mentioned earlier the contrast between Mr. Robinson's condemnation of Beara and other members of the VRS and Dr. Karadzic's rousing support for "my generals." Karadzic knows that he cannot accept the reality of what happened to the Srebrenica Muslims at the hands of the VRS because that condemns him, condemns the man who had his finger on the pulse of the operation from its very inception, who monitored it personally in the planning stages, who issued instructions to move the prisoners from the last arguable place they might have had a chance to the place where there was no reason for them to be other than to be executed; the man who had to approve any change in the operations that would allow Muslim men and boys to get out alive; the man whose top officials travelled to the area and reported back to him, who chortled over the reburials that seemingly would prevent the world from ever knowing what really happened, who created transparently sham "investigations" as a laughable fig leaf to cover his tracks. He knows the truth of his responsibility is exposed by the totality of this overwhelming evidence and so he seeks to treat each piece in isolation or irrationally deny them. Your Honours, in the case of the Srebrenica component, as in the totality of the case, Dr. Karadzic's ceaseless efforts to justify, deflect, obfuscate, mis-characterise, and outright misrepresent have culminated in the submissions we've just discussed, in which sweeping and unsupported generalisations are juxtaposed with citations that misrepresent or invert facts or even invent a new reality. These were not the flailing attempts of an uneducated man but of a man desperate to deny the facts that condemn him. These facts reveal beyond a reasonable doubt his guilt on all counts of the indictment. Mr. President, that would conclude the submissions except for the remaining question by the Court about Count 7. The Court had inquired about deportation in relation to the municipalities and the mens rea in connection with that, so I would turn first, of course, to Count 7 which indicates at paragraph 68 the commission of forcible transfer and deportation from the municipalities, those municipalities are defined in Count 3 at paragraph 48, as the Court is aware. Insofar as the mens rea is concerned, forcible transfer is the forcible displacement of persons which may take place within national borders. That was found by the Stakic appeals judgement at paragraph 317. Whereas the crime of deportation requires a displacement of individuals across a border, either a de jure border or displacement across a de facto border, the determination of which is a case-by-case determination based on the circumstances. As far as the mens rea is concerned, in the case of forcible transfer, since the ultimate location doesn't form a part of the elements, the mens rea is established by virtue of the intent to forcibly displace the individual. In the case of deportation, since displacement across a border is an element, the mens rea must encompass that element and the Prosecution must establish that the accused intended to displace the person across a de jure or de facto border.
