utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellencies. Good afternoon. For a minute it is afternoon. [Interpretation] Distinguished Mr. Tieger presented a series of points to prove that the position of the Defence is inaccurate and incorrect, but Mr. Tieger knows very well his own case and the documents that he himself had tendered too well to be able to say such things. For instance, he says that I was against introducing the state of war so that non-Serbs who had left and all sorts of refugees could not return. This is very far from being true. Just one example. 5970, a session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska, pages -- 5970 -- P970, P970. So on pages 37, 104, 110, and 111, I was talking about the reasons why the state of war was not being introduced. For instance, on page 110, let me read it in English. [In English] "Reserves, emotional reserves, material reserves, all that, all this has been preserved, moral reserves, all this has been preserved because we did not drill the nation. I know that every army in the world would like the entire nation to march in a file. They would not endure for long, that would be a very brief march indeed. The nation would crumble down. Therefore, let us not go into political matters. We are here in the Assembly. We can submit an official request to the Assembly to introduce a state of war. This Assembly has rejected that several times. I do not want to introduce it and I did not introduce it at a certain point at -- and I did introduce it at a certain point under constitutional power ..." and so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, is that a B/C/S page number, 110?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English it's 110 and 111, towards the bottom of page 110 and the beginning of 111.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Late Professor Koljevic on page 258 says again in our position to request for a state of war: [In English] "The civilian authority believes that the army acting on the idea of the state of war wants to take over all power in its hands." [Interpretation] Those were the real reasons and it has nothing to do with the return of refugees. You will find references in other Assembly sessions and in interviews where I say that I don't want the people's life to be militarised. It's also mentioned on page 37 that the war is of low intensity, what would things look like if Israel introduced a state of war because of a low-intensity war with the PLO. Those were the analogies I used. And the fact that this did not have anything to do with the return of refugees -- first of all, in the Assembly I often had to seek approval and consent for very embarrassing things and in those cases, political speeches had a pacifying tone. But these things do not govern the return of refugees. The return of refugees was governed by agreements that I signed guaranteed by the international community. That is what counts, not the words of an Assemblyman or my words in response to him to calm the situation down. But look at our final brief concerning the return of refugees. That's page 257, paragraphs 996; paragraphs 989 to 999 of our final brief. And of course it is expected that if refugees return, two groups of refugees would not meet in Zvornik. Somebody has to guarantee the Serbs' safety if they were to return there. There is nothing wrong with a two-way process. On page 3 of today's transcript it is said that President Karadzic did not declare a state of war to make return impossible; however, in paragraph 999 of our final brief we quote an example, namely, the example of Bijeljina where refugees returned at my invitation and it turned out to be a little premature and it turned out to cause certain problems. So this argument of the Prosecution is completely worthless. And the evidence that we have support the assertions of the Defence and support our case. On page 5 Mr. Tieger says: Give Zvornik to Muslims. Give Zvornik to Muslims does not mean that Muslims would come to Zvornik; it means put Zvornik in the Muslim entity, in the Muslim constituent unit. The two things have nothing in common. We are fighting for Zvornik to remain in our republic, not for Muslims not to return. On page 7 it is wrongly stated that I accepted the maps. We should review the tapes and you will see that I did not claim that. Regarding maps and that agreement, that agreement was the sine qua non of Bosnian independence. We made that perfectly clear and Europe accepted that and somebody wanted to cheat us. No. That won't do. We lived on 65 to 70 per cent of the territory, we were a sovereign, constituent people, we accepted that they exit Yugoslavia but only on the condition that we get something. That was a condition sine qua non. Serbs are not fools. Karadzic has nothing to do with it, not even the last granny in the last village in Bosnia would accept something like that. The record says that I accepted the maps, but the maps were the only thing that we did not accept. Our only condition was that maps had to be final, definitive, so that people do not flee from places where they expected they could go on living. The maps were in dispute and the evidence is replete with proof that maps needed to be finalised as soon as possible by working groups; however, that did not happen, not because of any failure on our part but because the Muslim side left that table. It says here that the principles were unacceptable to Karadzic because BH would have been a unified state. BH would not have been acceptable either to Serbs or Croats as a unitary state, even if we were a minority. Instead we were a large Christian majority of over 60 per cent. So this is not true either. Now, look at page T33968, where Ambassador Cutileiro mentions the diary of Ambassador Okun and the discussion with the foreign minister, Pinheiro. It says the only possible variant is a tripartite Bosnia. That was also our own condition. We accepted that with a heavy heart, but we did accept it. Ambassador Okun notes: [In English] Okun's notes indicate that he stated that it was absurd to blame the situation in Bosnia exclusively on the Serbs. [Interpretation] And on page 3396 it says that: [In English] "Cutileiro still posed the following a rhetorical question: Could we have a unitary Bosnia or did we have to have a tripartite Bosnia?" [Interpretation] And of course the foreign minister repeated on many occasions in the media that only a tripartite Bosnia could be a solution to the problem, so that is not correct either. Now, concerning statistics, I did not do the statistics. It was their own expert, Mrs. Tabeau. I was talking about proportionality. The number of Muslims that were there at the time of Dayton Accords, a large percentage left after that. I did not deal with proportions; it was Mrs. Tabeau's report that dealt with it. On the 31st of March, 1992, when the Muslim operation against Bijeljina -- Karadzic was away. It is said that the objective could have been achieved by different means. Of course every objective can be achieved by different means, and Ambassador Cutileiro writes that in his letter to the International Herald Tribune and repeats in all his speeches that it was a huge shame that war happened, bringing with it a huge loss of life, whereas everything could have been resolved by his Lisbon Agreement and the Cutileiro Plan. Perhaps it was not the IHT, perhaps it was The Economist. So it could have been done by different means, and Karadzic was in favour of different means. And Patrick Treanor, an expert and an employee of this OTP, says so, and we deal with it in our final brief in paragraph 101, where we state that Treanor agreed that up to 27 March 1992 until the outbreak of war, Karadzic had always advocated peace and peaceful solutions; he never advocated war. Mr. Treanor said that on page 14442. Mr. Treanor had worked in the OTP for 15 years and he was converted into an expert in order to translate the Prosecution case into evidence. He authored an important part of the pre-trial brief by his own admission, but he -- even he said that Karadzic had never advocated war before it broke out; he was against war. It doesn't cross OTP's mind to establish how the JCE could have been implemented, how could it have contained any element of removing non-Serbs from Republika Srpska without war. And even when the war broke out, the Prosecution neglects to notice our great efforts for combat to be avoided and to solve everything at the negotiating table. That was the point of all my speeches in the Assembly of Republika Srpska and elsewhere. Three signatures decide the fate of Bosnia, and in my platform it is clearly said there can be no fait accompli, there can be no recognition of territories taken with violence, and after the war everybody will return wherever they want. The Prosecution has - and we dealt with it in our final brief paragraphs 239 to 327 - 95 intercepts involving my conversations before the war and my speeches, that is to say, my words. I had given thousands of interviews and uttered millions of sentences and words, I rattled on the whole time, and they cannot find one single unmutilated sentence to use against me. 95 intercepts from the pre-war period and in all of them all they can find is my advocacy of peace and that is from my conversations with other members of the alleged JCE. They can only see how I advocated peace and how I tried to make Muslims safe and feel safe, how I tried to refrain from anything that could make them anxious, speeches in which peaceful coexistence is advocated. Let us be clear. If Muslims or Serbs or Croats wished a secular life, then we could live together. If any of these three peoples wanted to build their religion into the state machinery, then we could only live one next to another. And Mr. Izetbegovic and I agreed on that point completely. If Mr. Izetbegovic insisted on the Islamic Declaration and wanted to apply it to all the Muslims, we had nothing against it; but in that case, we would live each in their own canton. There is no inconsistency and no difference there. As for the war period, if the Prosecution says that a JCE can just crop up during the course of the war, although they cannot establish when and who did this, there are over 60 orders of mine, strictly confidential orders to organs that are supposed to implement them. That's no propaganda. In these 60 orders, they cannot find a single order that tolerates crimes or orders crimes. When Zupljanin is reporting that somebody is asking for as many civilians as possible to be gathered, he has a negative attitude towards that. There was no problem unless there was fighting, but then there were individual problems but that happens any time anywhere. In some European countries right now, only 30 to 40 homicides are being resolved when their state authorities are fully functioning now, in peacetime, and then we try to control everything, although we were totally destroyed, without an infrastructure, and without a proper state apparatus. Karavelic's statement was referred to here and due to my lack of experience I allowed that to be admitted because I kept thinking that he would come as a witness. And he says that SRK used artillery just as the 1st Corps of Bosnia-Herzegovina used it. Then later on this propaganda came, the Serbs did this, the Serbs did that, but there -- that is what he says throughout basically, that the SRK used artillery just as I used it, he said. Hospitals and other facilities that Karavelic refers to in his statement, he did not mention that these facilities were targeted only when they were used as military facilities. Why were enormous areas not targeted, large parts of different neighbourhoods where not a single shell fell? Why? Because no one ever fired from there. In 1995, the 4-year-old girl, she was not killed by a multiple rocket-launcher. Later on we'll have to move into closed session because we just have to deal with this now, whatever we can deal with in open court. Judge Baird asked the Muslim investigator why they did not deal with the horizontal deflection of the projectile in the street -- in Nehru Street and he had no answer to that. They came to the window, they saw where the Serb positions were, and that's what they inferred. This was not done. As for the vertical deflection, as stated Mr. Tieger here -- no, it was 70 centimetres in terms of height. That was the difference. So it was fired from elsewhere. It was not visible and it was not targeted. It was a stray bullet. That's why this isn't in the indictment, that's why it was thrown out of the indictment. At any rate, it is not the way it is being represented. The transcript does not reflect that this difference of 70 centimetres is the difference in height from the window to the wall and that is very clear there. There is 70 centimetres, that's how the bullet went and the dimensions of the room have to be taken into account as well. 100 sniper victims from Spicasta Stijena? Well, why is there not a single fatality in the indictment against me? This person was wounded, that person was wounded, but their experts also said - and the representatives of the UN said - that there were stray bullets everywhere, on all sides, and that more people were killed by stray bullets than by snipers. Snipers of the Serb army did not target civilians intentionally and not a single piece of evidence was presented to that effect. The distinguished Mr. Tieger tried to defend, from my objections, that is, witnesses of the Prosecution who were MUP investigators of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the same time. He says that KDZ166 did not make any mistakes during his investigations, and this allegedly refers to other investigators too. So let's deal with one particular example now. Let us look at G7. The investigation organs sketched the scene during the investigation and that's where they marked the cardinal point of north, and north is marked as perpendicular to the street of Oslobodilaca Sarajeva. According to the sketch of the scene, it does not correspond with the actual cardinal point of north, it actually has an azimuth that is approximately 300 degrees. So the police marked it wrongly. And 60 degrees is the mistake involved and that cannot be an acceptable error. When I asked that witness here in court, when I say: Where is the north here? And then his answer is: Well, whichever way you look at it. No, it's not the way it's done. The north is always marked on maps, but what was needed was to accuse the Serb side. Mirsad Sabljica tried to explain that north was marked properly on the sketch of this scene, but when confronted with evidence he corrected that and his assessment was that north constitutes an angle with Oslobodilaca Sarajeva of 30 to 35 degrees. That is what he said on page T7787 through 88. The exhibit is D741. KDZ166, who Mr. Tieger is trying to protect, agreed that the sketch was incorrect, but he could not explain why north was not marked properly. I wonder -- the reference is T8297 through 8300. I wonder in which one of our countries did the participants in this trial come from this kind of investigation would work. Is there any system or any country where this kind of investigation could be carried out and found acceptable? How can that be considered an established fact? There is lots of that, and many investigations and Muslim investigators themselves admitted that their investigations were not done according to the usual kind of procedure that was applied in peacetime. It was abbreviated. You can use that kind of thing in propaganda, but you cannot appear before a criminal court that way because this is an offence to the court itself. Turkusic, in relation to G19, that particular incident, testifies that the shell fell at 105 hundred hours [as interpreted], although CSB Sarajevo reports show that the first information about the shelling was received at 11.30 and the commission appeared on the scene at 12.15. T9064. So if this is not a mistake and if this is not sloppiness, then I really don't know what precision is. Also, the results of the investigation of the counter-sabotage unit of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina and UNPROFOR considerably vary in terms of the angle of descent and direction of fire.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not catch the transcript references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat the transcript page number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] T9066 through 69, and T9074 through 75. There are traces of fragments that do not correspond to the alleged explosion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not catch the numbers again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The alleged scene --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat the numbers again, if you said any.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript T9098. So the video representation of the incident shows that the positions of the alleged victims and wounded persons do not correspond to the version of the incident that is suggested. T096 to 9094 [as interpreted], those are the transcript references and T9100 to 9101. It is fully clear that investigations were carried out unprofessionally regarding Markale II, that incident, because the shells could not have come from Serb positions because, inter alia, and that was explained in our final brief, paragraph 2125 through 2162, and also for the reason that was omitted from our final brief and that is evidence to the effect that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps did not have mortars at these positions, the positions referred to by the Prosecution, because these mortars were in a completely different municipality. That is D2331, paragraph 51. Then D234, paragraph 24; D2344, paragraph 10; and D2451, paragraph 24; D2341, paragraph 24; and D2344, paragraph 10. So many distortions, so many concoctions of quasi evidence. It is highly advisable for the Trial Chamber to double-check everything that the Prosecution presented. Can we now please move into private session briefly because that is required by the subject matter involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please decide whether we're going to take a break or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we started at 12.00. You can continue until 1.00. How long do you expect to last?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I would need one and a half hours and that is definitely the time that I'm going to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you need, we'll take a break in the middle, if you like, for 15 or 20 minutes. I'll leave it to you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is agreeable. Maybe that would be good, to give me a chance to put my papers in order. [In English] Did you mean right now or ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I said I would leave it to you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yeah, I would be grateful for this break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then shall we begin at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Relating to item 1, genocide in municipalities, Mr. Tieger is now trying to distance himself from the Stakic, Brdjanin case, and the Krajisnik case, where the Trial Chamber acquitted the accused of the crime of genocide. He says that there were differences between the accused and that the accused had no jurisdiction over the army. However, that was not what he said when he wanted to take over thousands of adjudicated facts from these respective judgements. He tried to put the Chamber in a position in which it would believe that the interests of the accused coincided with Karadzic's interest in disputing the evidence including the evidence on the crimes and expulsion that are being attributed to the army. In these cases, the OTP presented allegations that the local organs led by Stakic and Brdjanin were closely co-operating with the army as part of the joint criminal enterprise with a view to committing genocide. This is only an attempt to distance the said accused from the conduct of the army, or rather, the Army of Republika Srpska in various municipalities in 1992; however, it's too late because the OTP had already taken a stance when these cases were tried. Had the OTP presented any new evidence relating to the Karadzic case, maybe that manoeuvre would have been successful. However, they failed to put forth any new evidence. They are presenting the same facts, the same speeches, the same incidents that had been found by previous Trial Chambers insufficient to return a verdict for genocide in the municipalities, both in this Tribunal and before the International Court of Justice. These elements were never accepted as being part of the intention to destroy Bosnian Muslims. The OTP would like to have a conclusion on genocide intentions deriving from forcible relocation; however, the evidence about forcible relocation speak something completely different. Both Mr. Tieger and the OTP never explained why, if there was an intention to destroy the Muslims of Bosnia, why so many of these Muslims who were under the control of Bosnian Serbs, who were detained and interrogated and were living in these villages and in municipalities throughout 1992 and later on, why were they allowed to leave? That was not a forcible transfer. We can counter evidence with one another. If the aim was to have them destroyed, why was it made possible for them to be entered into lists, why buses were paid for, allowing them to leave wherever they wanted to go? None of this convinced either the International Court of Justice or the Trial Chamber of this Tribunal that there was any force applied in municipalities that was calculated to destroy this group of people, albeit there was a possibility for that but it was never established. The Prosecution failed to prove genocide in the form as stipulated in Count 1. Today the OTP said that I said about Mr. Harland that it was untrue that he came to defend the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that he was not impartial. During my negotiations with his superiors, Mr. Harland took notes. Some of his superiors testified here, including General Rose, but first and foremost those involved in political negotiations such as Ambassador Akashi and Cutileiro. The OTP never asked me about their attitudes because they knew to the minutest detail what I was able to accept. Instead, they asked Harland, who was totally incompetent to testify about these things. He has no military background, but nevertheless he proposed the theory about three forms of shelling. Concerning his impartiality, this is a disaster. On page 2128, this man said that the Security Council Resolutions 824, 819, and 836 called for the withdrawal of all forces except those of the BH government. Of course, all the gestures of the Army of Republika Srpska he has to consider as illegitimate because he didn't know that we were equal. This is still the case there; however, he maintains that everybody else except the BH government forces should withdraw. This is an additional reason confirming that he was here to defend the BH government, that the Serbs were outlaws, and that the government was right. Therefore, his entire testimony can and must be discarded, particularly the portion thereof in which he proffered his unprofessional opinion that he is not trained to give. He was not the only one. There are plenty similar to his case. Banbury admitted the tricks of Army of BH army --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the transcript page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 28 of today's transcript. It is also said there that it was misrepresented that Harland did not have a clue what to do. Banbury, however, admitted that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina resorted to tricks. Neither of them knew anything about the UN Resolutions. Every new replacement, any new staff, came with ready-made prejudices and without proper knowledge. Although Mr. Banbury was in the habit of educating others about the UN mandate, and you can see from his testimony that he didn't know anything about it but rather had completely wrong knowledge. Harland also demonstrated the lack of knowledge about the Army of BH even though we presented a host of documents about the conduct of the BH army, about the fire that was coming from their side of course. He considered all of that to be legitimate and he didn't see the need to record that because it was done by a legitimate government in his view. We are now on page 29, where Mr. Tieger says that Janc's list did not include the persons who had previously been killed, and the reason for that is that he had purged that list. He didn't know where these people had come from. He discarded hundreds of exhumed bodies. The OTP argues that everyone who was listed in that area was shot dead. Even Janc admitted that that was not the case because all the other documents show that a huge number of people were exhumed, not from three graves, according to Janc, but from each and every grave. They were -- those who were killed in 1992, 1993, 1994 were exhumed from common graves. It is totally pointless and senseless to claim that if there are 900 bodies in a secondary grave, nobody can establish where the primary grave was. These are the differences that cannot be legally accepted, and these are the routes taken by the column during the breakthrough. So these were primary graves. So if there's 13 per cent or 10 per cent, that can be a secondary grave. For all others, it was a primary grave. With regard to the 10th Sabotage Detachment, Mr. Tieger said that Erdemovic testified about the detachment that had only a few of them. When asked how it was kept secret for such a long time and who he was allowed to discuss this, he said: Everybody except a few associates who wouldn't say this to Pelemis. And that's what this revealed later when Salapura gave testimony. At the time, Erdemovic was not allowed to discuss this issue in order to prevent it being disclosed to Pelemis who was somewhere in hospital at the time. And this is a fact. On page 33, Mr. Tieger said, concerning surface remains in two locations, these surface remains that were discovered by Mrs. Albright after she had been brought there and shown it. They're definitely, most definitely, not the result of mass execution. These must have been remains of those who were involved in combat. It was neither a mass nor an execution and it is crystal clear for us that we need to have an investigation. Mr. Tieger, however, says that there was no intention of conducting an investigation. I resigned in May and I was no longer able to follow what was going on with those investigations. On page 35, Mr. Tieger says: Is it possible that all the institutions, such as the army, et cetera, ignored the president's or the supreme commander's requests? When an army is doing something, they make a plan, they take a decision, they issue a preparatory and executive order, and they monitor the implementation, then they assign specific unit for carrying out these orders. The people were begging at the time: Can you tell me -- can you send me ten people or 15 people? They were pleading with the MUP to give them manpower to carry out certain jobs. That is not how an army operates. That was not the army's attitude. Yes, some individuals can do that, but the army not. The army takes decisions differently and executes them differently. There was not a word from the Prosecution about the evidence of KW586, which sheds very clear light on the events, the behaviour and the tricks that were supposed to stigmatise us at the time for the purpose of obtaining an international military intervention; however, the matter ended up in court, which I believe is an insult to the Tribunal. Thus, many of the 234 witnesses whom they believed had lied did not even try to minimise it. This concerns forcible transfer and they can't quite agree on that. From Bosanska Krupa and the Krupa on the Una river from the Serbian bank, from the Serbian side, the authorities moved Muslims from one village to another village in the same municipality and some of them they moved to the Sanski Most municipality, to the Muslim village to Tomina, to save them from the combat zone. And Vojko Klickovic was acquitted before the Military Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina for these incidents and this is a court that very rarely acquits a Serb. Also from Bosanski Novi people were given the choice of going to Banja Luka. They didn't want to. In fact, they tried, they reached Doboj and then they returned. All of them wanted to go to third countries. Certainly they were not happy to do it, but it is quite clear that this was not forcible transfer. This was an attempt to accommodate people because the situation required it. Of course, one has to bear in mind that both Doboj and Banja Luka are in Republika Srpska. It's not only in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's in Republika Srpska. And I have to thank Mr. Tieger that for the purposes of his case he declared the borders of Republika Srpska to be state borders. Now when he needs to claim that the transfer of civilians from Republika Srpska to the Muslim-Croat Federation, he says it's moving to another state. So anything goes. And this brings us to Markale -- excuse me, we are still on Srebrenica. Mr. Tieger recalls that Beara referred to two presidents or two chiefs; however, KDZ320, a witness for the Prosecution, testified that Beara wanted to create the impression -- in fact, he wanted to impress others that he was duty-bound towards some commanders, but the witness himself did not believe it and he could not find any connection with President Karadzic. Also Franz Kos, who also testified here, never heard any reference to President Karadzic as having ordered that his unit get involved in any crime, i.e., executions. When it comes to speculations as to where the prisoners were supposed to go, it is said that nobody knows it was to be Batkovic prison. I remember that it was mentioned in the transcripts, but we don't have the audio recording; however, Milenko Todorovic said that at the time he had been told to get ready to accept in Batkovici a large number of prisoners. It was cancelled two or three days later, perhaps even five or six days, but the fact is that the initial intention was clear, namely, that these prisoners would go to Batkovic. Earlier on - and I can't help mentioning this - Mr. Tieger said that Robert Frost had asked me about 2.000 people -- sorry, David Frost. Robert Frost is a poet, the poet who even said that good fences make good friends. So David Frost was not asking me about those 2.000 whose whereabouts were known; he was asking me about 15.000 people who were somewhere in the woods. However, Mr. Tieger wants to create the impression that I knew their whereabouts and didn't want to say. I didn't know. All I knew was that they were somewhere in the forests, and everybody knew that. Similarly, the Prosecution tries to shake the Defence case, which cannot be shaken, by bits and pieces of sentences or misquotes. Mr. Allsop did not say what he is claimed to have said. On T29509, Mr. Allsop was asked: Even if his report were to be accepted and including the argument that the trajectory of the projectile was affected in some way as to cause a margin of error of 50 centimetres, or rather, a deviation of 50 centimetres before hitting the ground, this would correspond to a margin of error of 33 per cent. He answered "yes." But this discussion involved only the variables between the time when the projectile hit the ground and the 50 centimetres that it travelled before impacting. Dr. Allsop testified that such a variable, such as wind, humidity, the nature of the soil, do affect the angle at which the projectile would impact the ground. However, the question did not apply to other fundamental objections such as the impossibility of calculating the angle of descent at Markale I because the stabiliser was moved before measurements were taken. The stabiliser was taken out and the crater was damaged. It was especially impossible the following day when Zecevic came. It was not only Allsop who confirmed it; it was confirmed by all the investigators from the United Nations and they said it was impossible to determine the angle of descent once the stabiliser is moved or removed from its original place. The margin of error has no meaning if the site has been tampered with. UN representatives even offered a very generous margin of error. If it had been possible, the UN would have broadened the margin to blame the Serbs; however, they didn't do it. Allsop and the United Nations representatives and all their inquiries and investigations show that it is inaccurate and incorrect to ascribe responsibility to the Serbs and Dr. Karadzic on the basis of what one volunteer, Berko Zecevic, determined subsequently. Your Excellencies, the Prosecution is unable to find in the fundamental documents of Republika Srpska any evidence. The Republika Srpska from its very beginnings acted based on documents and decisions, not on the basis of bits and pieces of sentences. It produced the constitution, laws, decisions, declarations, proposals, and bylaws. The government adopted a large number of laws and decisions. And after December 1992, the president himself issued a large number of orders and decisions, both public and confidential, including appeals. This Office of the Prosecutor did not find one fundamental document to prove that the Serb people had intended to affect what exactly happened. We knew what would happened and we begged: Let's not go into civil war. It was clear at that time that everything could have been resolved peacefully, that Serbs were for it. Witness Cutileiro testified that very early on, while Karadzic was still at the conference, before 14 August 1992, Karadzic was prepared to cede a lot of territory in order to save peace. There is an abundance of evidence. Croatia clearly at that time had racist laws. It's clear why so many Serbs and Jews suffered at their hands. Republika Srpska did not have any such laws. Directive 7 does not count because it was never implemented. Mladic changed it without me. If he -- if it had been my directive, he wouldn't have been allowed to change it without my approval. There is not a single word except occasional utterances by individual Assemblymen. I was forced to make political speeches. I had to make the Assembly swallow many bitter pills and convince them that we have to accept certain things, and these Assemblymen had every right to be angry. However, gentlemen, these were not enactments that underlie the behaviour of state agencies or officials. Debates among Assemblymen or newspaper stories also do not underlie the behaviour of a state. It is only the fundamental documents of the state that govern the state behaviour. I want to emphasise -- God forbid that the Serbian leadership had been different, that it had not included so many prominent professors, academicians, doctors, and others. God knows what the war would have looked like then. But none of what happened was a product of the behaviour of the state. And we have ample evidence that people who wanted to live in peace would have been able to live in peace pending a political solution. The war did not happen as I wanted it. It was horrible and let's hope to God that it was the last, but that is not in my power. I expect and I trust that the Chamber will study carefully every document and every exhibit, both from the Defence and the Prosecution, and if that happens, I have no doubt that a judgement of acquittal will follow. I apologise to everyone for my amateurism, but my thirst for the truth is much stronger than my legal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless there are matters to be raised further, we will soon adjourn and the Chamber will withdraw to deliberate on the evidence received throughout the proceedings. The size of this case has been unprecedented. The first Prosecution witness testified on the 13th of April, 2010, and the last Defence witness testified on the 20th of February, 2014. Over the course of these four years, the Chamber received the evidence of close to 600 witnesses and admitted more than 11.500 exhibits, which amounts to over 146.000 pages. The volume of filings submitted by all parties in this case has reached 90.000 pages and 48.000 transcript pages record the course of hearings during the trial. Notwithstanding the sheer magnitude of the case, thanks to the co-operation of the parties and the professionalism demonstrated by everyone involved, the proceedings ran smoothly. Therefore, on behalf of the Chamber, I wish to start by thanking the parties for the professionalism they have demonstrated throughout. My thanks also extend to the standby counsel and his team. I now turn to our court deputy and ushers and wish to express my gratitude for their assistance through the course of the trial. The Chamber thanks the interpreters and the court reporters who have had an extremely difficult task. We thank Audio and Visual Unit, ITSS, as well as the Victims and Witnesses Section, the Security Section, and the Dutch police. The Chamber also wishes to thank all the States who have co-operated during these proceedings pursuant to Rule 54 bis. Last, but not least, I will now turn to our legal staff, without whose assistance the conduct of the proceedings would not have been possible. I would like to name them one by one on the record in order express our gratitude. First, those who have now left the case or the ICTY: Lorna Davidson, Linda Murnane, Grant Dawson, Rachel Opie, Steven Koh, Amy Eussen, and Aurelie Roche-Mair. Next, those who are still with us: Nolwenn Guibert, Silva Hinek, Viviana de la Pena Escobar, Nakako Onishi, Harshan Athureliya, Sun Kim, Kirsten Calhoun, Christine Keller, and Cliff Farhang. We have also received the invaluable assistance of fellows: Alia El Khatib, Nak-Hee Hyun, Kyunghwa Min, Jooheon Lee, Jaemin Choung, and Harin Song, as well as the contribution of 70 legal interns. I thank them all for their work and dedication to the Chamber and these proceedings. Finally, we also thank our respective secretaries for their dedicated assistance. Now, pursuant to Rule 87 of the Tribunal's Rules, I declare the hearing closed. The Chamber will withdraw to deliberate in private and will issue a Scheduling Order for the pronouncement of the judgement in due course. We stand adjourned.
